doc.title: Doug Carn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 24, 2023

title: His mother's gigs with Dizzy Gillespie and her band
summary: His mother played Dizzy Gillespie's gig in Harlem, later gigged locally, and Carn's first gig was with her band.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you, before I forget, did you think it was really hip that your mother played with Dizzy Gillespie a couple of times?

Extremely hip. And she didn’t tell me that until I got older you know. I was probably about 40 when she told me that. But what had happened was she was in Harlem. She’d go up to Harlem during the summer and stay with Uncle T which was my grand-uncle, my grandmama’s brother, and work you know. But she would also go up there to go to Juilliard which I didn’t know. But she got into a summer program where she’d go to Juilliard and rehearse you know. Yeah, she had a friend from a talent show at the Apollo and so mama played for her and the girl won. And Dizzy was one of the judges. And so Dizzy paid her a compliment and invited her to a gig of his, I think it was at the Harlem YMCA. But anyway she went and the piano player didn’t show so the guy was acting like he didn’t want to pay Diz because he didn’t have a band. And so they said, “There’s a piano player right there, come on, baby.” So my mama made the gig. Then she played another one, then he called her again and she wouldn’t go ‘cause I was sick you know. So he didn’t call her no more after that.
I like that term, “My mama made the gig.”

And then she was gigging anyway. As a matter of fact my first gig was with the band she was with before I started the New Tones you know. Because she could read music so if they wanted to play “All the Things You Are” or “Stella by Starlight,” she would play it correctly and she knew that she played it, and the chords over and over again, the same structure. But they kept being after her about soloing you know. And she didn’t want to solo. She didn’t want to improvise. She didn’t want to play something and not know what she was playing. She was that kind of musician you know, that I’m not playing nothing that I don’t know what I’m playing, that was her point of view you know.
